content: #4 I rephrased a key motivational phrase. As it was, it implied one fixed a map B→CB\to CB→C and then allowed the family A#B→CA\#B\to CA#B→C to vary when looking for it, whereas of course we want the family to be fixed.
subject: Diagonal argument redux

content:
#5 I guess I should thrash out why it’s worth thinking of F ⁣:A#B→CF\colon A\#B\to CF:A#B→C as being a family of morphisms B→CB\to CB→C. Given any a ⁣:X→Aa\colon X\to Aa:X→A, hence supposedly picking out one such morphism, then for any p ⁣:Y→X∈C/Xp\colon Y\to X \in \mathcal{C}/Xp:Y→X∈C/X and b ⁣:Y→Bb\colon Y\to Bb:Y→B we get

Y→δY#Y→p#idYX#Y→a#bA#B→FC(1) Y\xrightarrow{\delta} Y\# Y \xrightarrow{p\# \mathrm{id}_Y} X\# Y \xrightarrow{a\# b} A \# B \xrightarrow{F} C\qquad (1) Yδ​Y#Yp#idY​​X#Ya#b​A#BF​C(1)

So, if we think of aaa as being an element of AAA at stage XXX, then for any later stage YYY (via ppp), we have an assignment of elements b↦F(p∗a,b)b\mapsto F(p^*a,b)b↦F(p∗a,b).

I want to think of this, for fixed aaa, as some kind of map of presheaves with codomain the representable given by CCC, but I’d have to think exactly how. Thinking out loud, I have two presheaves (C/X)op→Cop→Set(\mathcal{C}/X)^{\mathrm{op}} \to \mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{op}} \to {\mathrm{Set}}(C/X)op→Cop→Set, namely X∗y(B) ⁣:(Y→X)↦C(Y,B)X^*y(B)\colon (Y\to X) \mapsto \mathcal{C}(Y,B)X∗y(B):(Y→X)↦C(Y,B) and X∗y(C) ⁣:(Y→X)↦C(Y,C)X^*y(C)\colon (Y\to X) \mapsto \mathcal{C}(Y,C)X∗y(C):(Y→X)↦C(Y,C). If I’ve done my calculation correct, (1)(1)(1) above seems like it gives a natural transformation Fa ⁣:X∗y(B)⇒X∗y(C) ⁣:(C/X)op→SetF_a\colon X^*y(B) \Rightarrow X^*y(C) \colon (\mathcal{C}/X)^{\mathrm{op}} \to {\mathrm{Set}}Fa​:X∗y(B)⇒X∗y(C):(C/X)op→Set with component (Y→X)↦((Y→B)↦(1))(Y\to X) \mapsto \big( (Y\to B) \mapsto (1) \big)(Y→X)↦((Y→B)↦(1)). So the intuition that FFF is a family of maps B→CB\to CB→C seems to hold up, at some level.
subject: Diagonal argument redux

content:
#6 The notes are somewhat expanded now, including the material from #5.

Since Lawvere arrives at the diagonal argument as the contrapositive of his fixed-point theorem, it’s worth thinking about whether what I have in my notes arises as the contrapositive of some sensible fixed-point theorem. One thing that is a little odd in my notes is that the notion of incomplete parametrisation A#B→CA\#B\to CA#B→C deals with external maps B→CB\to CB→C, rather than general X#B→CX\#B\to CX#B→C, which in the cartesian closed setting would correspond to the rather natural generalised points X→CBX\to C^BX→CB. On the other hand, asking whether all external maps are captured by an internal parametrisation seems reasonably natural.

We can then try to define a complete parametrisation A#B→CA\#B \to CA#B→C, as follows

for every B→CB\to CB→C there is a X→aAX\xrightarrow{a} AXa​A such that for all Y→pXY\xrightarrow{p} XYp​X and Y→bBY\xrightarrow{b} BYb​B we have f∘b=F∘((p∗a)#b)∘δ ⁣:Y→Cf\circ b = F\circ ((p^*a)\#b) \circ \delta\colon Y\to Cf∘b=F∘((p∗a)#b)∘δ:Y→C.

Then we can prove, following Lawvere, that if A#A→CA\#A\to CA#A→C is a complete parametrisation, every σ ⁣:C→C\sigma\colon C\to Cσ:C→C has a fixed point, in the sense that there is a Y→cCY\xrightarrow{c} CYc​C with σ∘c=c\sigma\circ c = cσ∘c=c. We take ccc to be X→aA→δA#A→FC→σCX\xrightarrow{a} A \xrightarrow{\delta} A\# A \xrightarrow{F} C\xrightarrow{\sigma} CXa​Aδ​A#AF​Cσ​C, where we take aaa as in the above definition (and p=idXp=\mathrm{id}_Xp=idX​). This seems to be the result whose contrapositive is then the diagonal argument I give, though if I’m trying to convince people who love substructural logics, the direct proof I give of the diagonal argument is better.

However, I’m not 100% satisfied with the definition of complete parametrisation, since in principle, the statement after the existential quantifier could be satisfied by taking YYY to be an initial object, assuming one exists. What is missing is the notion of ‘display maps’ or covers: in a topos, the epimorphisms Y→1Y\to 1Y→1. It’s not clear how one should interpret this. Clearly, in the proof of the fixed-point theorem, if one constructs a ‘fixed point’ 0→C0\to C0→C with 000 initial, then that’s not so exciting! As in the explanation in #5, one would hope that examining what is happening with the slice categories and presheaves, it might shed some illumination. Other than that, I guess I need to knuckle down and find an interesting application/example, to see what’s going on. Harley Eades III had a proposal to look at magmoidal categories as underlying various substructural logics and interactions with dependent type theory, along the lines of how linear and dependent types can be made to interact, so it’s possible he has some ideas in this space.
subject: Diagonal argument redux

content:
#7 Taking the presheaf view as in #5, an incomplete parametrisation is a map F ⁣:A#B→CF\colon A\#B\to CF:A#B→C such that there exists f ⁣:B→Cf\colon B\to Cf:B→C such that for no a ⁣:X→Aa\colon X\to Aa:X→A is X∗f=FaX^*f = F_aX∗f=Fa​. But FFF is complete parametrisation if for every f ⁣:B→Cf\colon B\to Cf:B→C there is a ⁣:X→Aa\colon X\to Aa:X→A with X∗f=FaX^*f = F_aX∗f=Fa​.

Notice that there is a subtlety in that the first quantifier is external: it quantifies over the hom-set of the category, but the following ones are essentially in the internal logic, such that it is. Moreover, the (“internal”) existential quantifier in the definition of complete parametrisation doesn’t have much to work with, as opposed to in a regular category, where existentials work fine, one has regular epimorphisms alpenty. More generally, one could ask that one has a regular epi to interpret ∃\exists∃, but in this case we are starting from the empty context; if there is a terminal object we could ask for X→1X\to 1X→1 to be regular epi, but I haven’t assumed that. It may be that to get a sensible, contentful statement of Lawvere’s fixed-point theorem I should assume more than what I have…
subject: Diagonal argument redux
